narrative:
The model predicted a 72% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your undergraduate GPA was the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. At 2.60, it sits noticeably below the 3.23 average of students who were accepted, signaling weaker academic preparation in the eyes of the model. Next, your family income bracket of upper-middle class contributed in the same direction, though with less force; while this bracket is common among accepted students, the model interpreted your specific combination of background and academics as increasing risk. Finally, your first-year law school decile ranking of 7.00 worked against you as well. Although this is slightly better than the accepted-student average of 6.00, it still added to the overall prediction of failure.

Taken together, these elements led the model to conclude you were unlikely to pass the bar on the first try. To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance in the coming year and consider targeted bar-prep resources that address gaps in foundational knowledge. Strengthening your record in these areas could meaningfully shift future predictions in your favor. (218 words)
